claim: Dysfunction of noradrenergic (NE) neurons is implicated in the pathogenesis of bipolar disorder (BPD).
source: Dysfunction of the noradrenergic (NE) neurons is implicated in the pathogenesis of bipolar disorder (BPD).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information without specific data from this study.

claim: ErbB4 is highly expressed in NE neurons.
source: ErbB4 is highly expressed in NE neurons
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to prior literature.

claim: Genetic variation of ErbB4 has been linked to BPD.
source: its genetic variation has been linked to BPD
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Conditional deletion of ErbB4 in locus coeruleus (LC) NE neurons increases neuronal spontaneous firing through NMDA receptor hyperfunction.
source: conditional deletion of ErbB4 in locus coeruleus (LC) NE neurons increases neuronal spontaneous firing through NMDA receptor hyperfunction
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing increased firing rates and NMDA receptor currents in mutant mice.

claim: Conditional deletion of ErbB4 in LC NE neurons elevates catecholamines in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
source: conditional deletion of ErbB4 in locus coeruleus (LC) NE neurons increases neuronal spontaneous firing through NMDA receptor hyperfunction, and elevates catecholamines in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC measurements showing increased norepinephrine and dopamine in CSF.

claim: Erbb4-deficient mice present mania-like behaviors, including hyperactivity, reduced anxiety and depression, and increased sucrose preference.
source: Erbb4-deficient mice present mania-like behaviors, including hyperactivity, reduced anxiety and depression, and increased sucrose preference.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tests including open field, elevated plus maze, forced swim, and sucrose preference tests.

claim: Mania-like behaviors in Erbb4-deficient mice are completely rescued by the anti-manic drug lithium.
source: These behaviors are completely rescued by the anti-manic drug lithium or antagonists of catecholaminergic receptors.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tests showing normalization of behaviors after lithium treatment.

claim: Mania-like behaviors in Erbb4-deficient mice are completely rescued by antagonists of catecholaminergic receptors.
source: These behaviors are completely rescued by the anti-manic drug lithium or antagonists of catecholaminergic receptors.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tests showing normalization of behaviors after treatment with prazosin and SCH23390.

claim: Concentrations of norepinephrine and its metabolites are significantly upregulated in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of BPD patients during the manic state.
source: For instance, the concentrations of norepinephrine and its metabolites are significantly upregulated in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of BPD patients during the manic state (Kurita, 2016; Manji et al., 2003; Post et al., 1973; Post et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Norepinephrine is downregulated in patients with depressive disorder.
source: In contrast, norepinephrine is downregulated in patients with depressive disorder (Maas et al., 1971; Moret and Briley, 2011; Wiste et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Norepinephrine is associated with mood transition in BPD patients.
source: and associated with mood transition in BPD patients (Kurita, 2016; Salvadore et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: ErbB4 plays a vital role in neural development, excitability, and synaptic plasticity.
source: ErbB4, a receptor tyrosine kinase, plays a vital role in a number of biological processes, including neural development, excitability, and synaptic plasticity (Mei and Nave, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons, ErbB4 is involved in the etiology of schizophrenia and epilepsy.
source: In parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons, ErbB4 is involved in the etiology of schizophrenia and epilepsy (Chen et al., 2010; Del Pino et al., 2013; Fisahn et al., 2009; Kx et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: ErbB4 mRNA is prominently expressed in locus coeruleus (LC) NE neurons.
source: ErbB4 mRNA is also prominently expressed in locus coeruleus (LC) NE neurons(Gerecke et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Coding variants of ERBB4 are genetically associated with BPD susceptibility.
source: and coding variants of ERBB4 are genetically associated with BPD susceptibility (Chen et al., 2012; Bipolar Genome Study et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic association studies.

claim: In the rostral part of the LC, approximately 40% of TH-positive neurons were Cre/Tomato-positive in Ai9;Th-Cre mice.
source: Colocalization analysis of TH staining and tdTomato suggested that in the rostral part of the LC, approximately 40% of TH-positive (TH+) neurons were Cre/Tomato-positive (Cre/Tomato+)
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In the rostral part of the LC, 92% of Cre/Tomato+ neurons were TH+ in Ai9;Th-Cre mice.
source: and 92% of Cre/Tomato+ neurons were TH+
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In the caudal part of the LC, Cre/Tomato+ neurons only constituted 14% of TH+ neurons in Ai9;Th-Cre mice.
source: whereas in the caudal part of the LC, Cre/Tomato+ neurons only constituted 14% of TH+ neurons
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In the caudal part of the LC, 82% of Cre/Tomato+ neurons were TH+ in Ai9;Th-Cre mice.
source: with 82% of Cre/Tomato+ neurons being TH+ (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The VTA and SNC contain approximately 70% of the dopaminergic neurons in the brain.
source: The VTA and SNC contain approximately 70% of the dopaminergic neurons in the brain (Björklund and Dunnett, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cre/Tomato was only expressed in approximately 1.6% and 0.9% of neurons in the rostral and caudal VTA, respectively, in Ai9;Th-Cre mice.
source: Cre/Tomato was only expressed in approximately 1.6% and 0.9% of neurons in the rostral and caudal VTA, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Only 2.1% of neurons in the rostral and caudal parts of the SNC were Cre/Tomato+ in Ai9;Th-Cre mice.
source: Moreover, only 2.1% of neurons in the rostral and caudal parts of the SNC were Cre/Tomato+.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In the rostral and caudal parts of the VTA and SNC, only 8% and 12% of Cre/Tomato+ neurons, respectively, were TH+ in Ai9;Th-Cre mice.
source: In the rostral and caudal parts of the VTA and SNC, only 8% and 12% of Cre/Tomato+ neurons, respectively, were TH+ (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: ErbB4 was significantly decreased in the LC of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Immunoblotting analysis showed that ErbB4 was significantly decreased in the LC of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice (Figure 1D,E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: No significant change in ErbB4 was detected in the midbrain (VTA and SNC) of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: with no significant change in the midbrain (VTA and SNC) (Figure 1D,E)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: No obvious changes in cell density or soma size of LC neurons were observed in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice compared to control mice.
source: In addition, we observed no obvious changes in cell density or soma size of LC neurons in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice compared to control mice (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: LC-NE neurons recorded from slices of control mice exhibited a firing rate of 1.94 ± 0.18 Hz.
source: Consistent with previous studies, LC-NE neurons recorded from slices of the control mice exhibited a firing rate of 1.94 ± 0.18 Hz (Chandler et al., 2014; Jedema and Grace, 2004) (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A,C and citations to prior studies.

claim: The spontaneous firing rate of LC-NE neurons in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice was significantly increased to 2.87 ± 0.18 Hz.
source: However, the spontaneous firing rate of LC-NE neurons in the Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice was significantly increased (2.87 ± 0.18 Hz) (Figure 2B,C)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The inter-spike interval of LC-NE neurons was significantly decreased in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: and the inter-spike interval was significantly decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Neuronal excitability can affect the expression and phosphorylation of TH.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that neuronal excitability can affect the expression and phosphorylation of TH, the rate limiting factor in catecholamine synthesis (Aumann et al., 2011; Chevalier et al., 2008; Lew et al., 1999; Zigmond et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: TH-Ser40 was markedly increased in the LC of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: We observed a marked increase in TH-Ser40 but not in total TH (Figure 2E,F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Total TH was not increased in the LC of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: We observed a marked increase in TH-Ser40 but not in total TH (Figure 2E,F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: DBH, NET, and COMT were unchanged in the LC of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: In contrast, DBH, another enzyme involved in norepinephrine synthesis, and NET and COMT, which regulate norepinephrine degradation, were unchanged (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: None of the norepinephrine-related proteins showed changes in the midbrain of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Using lysates from the midbrain, none of these proteins showed any changes (Figure 2G,H)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: LC-NE neurons are the major source of norepinephrine in the forebrain.
source: As LC-NE neurons are the major source of norepinephrine in the forebrain (Sara, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Norepinephrine concentration was significantly increased in the CSF of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Results showed that norepinephrine concentration was significantly increased in the CSF of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Dopamine concentration was significantly increased in the CSF of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Remarkably, the concentration of dopamine was also obviously increased compared with that in the control mice (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC measurements shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Dopamine is the precursor of norepinephrine.
source: Given that dopamine, the precursor of norepinephrine, is coupled with changes in norepinephrine level
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Dopamine can be co-released with norepinephrine by NE neurons.
source: and can be co-released with norepinephrine by NE neurons (Devoto et al., 2005; Guiard et al., 2008; Pozzi et al., 1994; Yamamoto and Novotney, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: An increase in glutamatergic synaptic input may contribute to the increased firing rate of LC-NE neurons.
source: An increase in glutamatergic synaptic input (Jodo and Aston-Jones, 1997; Somogyi and Llewellyn-Smith, 2001), or decrease in feedback inhibition from α-2-adrenoceptor, an autoreceptor (Langer, 1980; Starke, 2001), may contribute to the increased firing rate of LC-NE neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A decrease in feedback inhibition from α-2-adrenoceptor may contribute to the increased firing rate of LC-NE neurons.
source: An increase in glutamatergic synaptic input (Jodo and Aston-Jones, 1997; Somogyi and Llewellyn-Smith, 2001), or decrease in feedback inhibition from α-2-adrenoceptor, an autoreceptor (Langer, 1980; Starke, 2001), may contribute to the increased firing rate of LC-NE neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, the NMDA receptor, especially its subunit isoform NR2B, is regulated by ErbB4.
source: Moreover, in studies on the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, the NMDA receptor (NMDAR), especially its subunit isoform NR2B, is reported to be regulated by ErbB4 (Hahn et al., 2006; Pitcher et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The expression of NR2B was significantly increased in the LC of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Results showed that the expression of NR2B was significantly increased in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: No changes were detected in the expressions of NR1, A2A, A2C or NR2A in the LC of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: whereas no changes were detected in the expressions of NR1, A2A, A2C or NR2A (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: NMDAR-mediated current showed significantly increased amplitude in Ai9;Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice compared with Ai9;Th-Cre mice.
source: NMDAR-mediated current showed significantly increased amplitude in Ai9; Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice compared with Ai9; Th-Cre mice (Figure 3C,D)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Neither sEPSC nor sIPSC presented any changes in their amplitude or frequency in LC-NE neurons of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Neither sEPSC nor sIPSC presented any changes in their amplitude or frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intrinsic properties of LC-NE neurons were unchanged in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice compared with control mice.
source: In addition, intrinsic properties of LC-NE neurons measured by analysis of action potential (AP) threshold, AP amplitude, AP half-width, afterhyperpolarization (AHP), rheo-based current, Cm, Rin, and τ were unchanged compared with those of the control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The spontaneous firing rates and inter-spike intervals of LC-NE neurons in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice were rescued by the NMDAR antagonist APV.
source: Using the patch clamp technique, we found that the spontaneous firing rates and inter-spike intervals of LC-NE neurons in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice were rescued by the NMDAR antagonist APV (50 μM) (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3E–G.

claim: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice traveled longer distances in the open field test than control mice.
source: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice traveled longer distances and at higher speeds than control (ErbB4loxp/loxp) mice (Figure 4A–E)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4A–E.

claim: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice traveled at higher speeds in the open field test than control mice.
source: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice traveled longer distances and at higher speeds than control (ErbB4loxp/loxp) mice (Figure 4A–E)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4A–E.

claim: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice spent less time immobile in the open field test than control mice.
source: and spent less time immobile (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice spent more time in the open arms in the EPM test compared with control mice.
source: In the EPM, Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice spent more time in and presented more entries into the open arms compared with the control mice (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4G–I.

claim: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice presented more entries into the open arms in the EPM test compared with control mice.
source: In the EPM, Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice spent more time in and presented more entries into the open arms compared with the control mice (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4G–I.

claim: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice showed less immobility in the forced swim test compared with control mice.
source: In the forced swim test, Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice showed less immobility (Figure 4J)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice showed longer latency to first surrender in the forced swim test compared with control mice.
source: and longer latency to first surrender compared with the control mice (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice displayed increased preference for sucrose compared with control mice.
source: During this test, Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice displayed increased preference for sucrose compared with the control mice (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: No significant deficits in body weight were observed in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: No significant deficits in body weight or prepulse inhibition were observed in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant deficits in prepulse inhibition were observed in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: No significant deficits in body weight or prepulse inhibition were observed in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 52% of LC neurons were Cre/GFP-positive after AAV-Cre-GFP injection in Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Cre/GFP was expressed abundantly in the LC (Figure 5A), with 52% of LC neurons being Cre/GFP-positive (Cre/GFP+)
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly increased locomotor activity in the open field test.
source: In the open field test, viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly increased locomotor activity and traveling speed (Figure 5C,D)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly increased traveling speed in the open field test.
source: In the open field test, viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly increased locomotor activity and traveling speed (Figure 5C,D)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly increased the distance traveled at high speed in the open field test.
source: and both the distance and time traveled at high speed were significantly increased (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly increased the time traveled at high speed in the open field test.
source: and both the distance and time traveled at high speed were significantly increased (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly reduced immobility time in the open field test.
source: Moreover, the immobility time in the open area was significantly reduced (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly increased time in the open arms in the EPM test.
source: In the EPM, ErbB4 deletion in the LC significantly increased both the time in and number of entries into the open arms (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5H,I.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly increased number of entries into the open arms in the EPM test.
source: In the EPM, ErbB4 deletion in the LC significantly increased both the time in and number of entries into the open arms (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5H,I.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC decreased immobility time in the forced swim test.
source: In the forced swim test, mice with LC ErbB4 deletion exhibited decreased immobility time and increased latency to first surrender (Figure 5J,K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5J,K.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC increased latency to first surrender in the forced swim test.
source: In the forced swim test, mice with LC ErbB4 deletion exhibited decreased immobility time and increased latency to first surrender (Figure 5J,K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5J,K.

claim: Viral-mediated region-specific deletion of ErbB4 in the LC significantly increased sucrose preference.
source: In the sucrose preference test, LC ErbB4 deletion significantly increased sucrose preference of the injected mice (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Spontaneous excitability was increased in LC-NE neurons infected by AAV-Cre-GFP viruses in Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Spontaneous excitability (Figure 6A–C), NR2B expression (Figure 6D,E), and NMDAR-mediated current amplitude (Figure 6F,G) were increased in LC-NE neurons infected by AAV-Cre-GFP viruses in Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: NR2B expression was increased in LC-NE neurons infected by AAV-Cre-GFP viruses in Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Spontaneous excitability (Figure 6A–C), NR2B expression (Figure 6D,E), and NMDAR-mediated current amplitude (Figure 6F,G) were increased in LC-NE neurons infected by AAV-Cre-GFP viruses in Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: NMDAR-mediated current amplitude was increased in LC-NE neurons infected by AAV-Cre-GFP viruses in Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
source: Spontaneous excitability (Figure 6A–C), NR2B expression (Figure 6D,E), and NMDAR-mediated current amplitude (Figure 6F,G) were increased in LC-NE neurons infected by AAV-Cre-GFP viruses in Erbb4loxp/loxp mice.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: Lithium decreased locomotor activity of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the open field test.
source: In the open field test, lithium decreased locomotor activity, traveling speed, and distance and time traveled at high speed, and increased immobility time of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7A–E.

claim: Lithium decreased traveling speed of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the open field test.
source: In the open field test, lithium decreased locomotor activity, traveling speed, and distance and time traveled at high speed, and increased immobility time of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7A–E.

claim: Lithium decreased distance traveled at high speed of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the open field test.
source: In the open field test, lithium decreased locomotor activity, traveling speed, and distance and time traveled at high speed, and increased immobility time of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7A–E.

claim: Lithium decreased time traveled at high speed of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the open field test.
source: In the open field test, lithium decreased locomotor activity, traveling speed, and distance and time traveled at high speed, and increased immobility time of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7A–E.

claim: Lithium increased immobility time of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the open field test.
source: In the open field test, lithium decreased locomotor activity, traveling speed, and distance and time traveled at high speed, and increased immobility time of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7A–E.

claim: Lithium decreased time in the open arms by Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the EPM test.
source: In addition, lithium decreased both time in and entries into the open arms by Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the EPM (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7F–G.

claim: Lithium decreased entries into the open arms by Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the EPM test.
source: In addition, lithium decreased both time in and entries into the open arms by Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the EPM (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7F–G.

claim: Lithium-treated Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice exhibited significantly increased immobility time in the forced swim test.
source: The treated Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice also exhibited significantly increased immobility time and decreased latency to first surrender in the forced swim test (Figure 7H,I)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7H,I.

claim: Lithium-treated Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice exhibited decreased latency to first surrender in the forced swim test.
source: The treated Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice also exhibited significantly increased immobility time and decreased latency to first surrender in the forced swim test (Figure 7H,I)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7H,I.

claim: Lithium-treated Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice exhibited reduced sucrose preference in the sucrose preference test.
source: and reduced sucrose preference in the sucrose preference test (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The NR2B protein level was significantly decreased in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice receiving lithium.
source: The NR2B protein level and phosphorylation of TH were significantly decreased in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice receiving lithium (Figure 7K,L)

claim: Phosphorylation of TH was significantly decreased in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice receiving lithium.
source: The NR2B protein level and phosphorylation of TH were significantly decreased in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice receiving lithium (Figure 7K,L)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7K,L.

claim: No change was observed in the protein levels of TH, MB-COMT, or S-COMT in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice after lithium treatment.
source: whereas no change was observed in the protein levels of TH or the membrane-bound and soluble forms of COMT (MB-COMT and S-COMT, respectively) (Figure 7K,L).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7K,L.

claim: The spontaneous firing rates of LC-NE neurons in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice were rescued after lithium treatment.
source: In addition, the spontaneous firing rates and inter-spike intervals of LC-NE neurons in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice were both rescued after lithium treatment (Figure 7M,N).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7M,N.

claim: The inter-spike intervals of LC-NE neurons in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice were rescued after lithium treatment.
source: In addition, the spontaneous firing rates and inter-spike intervals of LC-NE neurons in Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice were both rescued after lithium treatment (Figure 7M,N).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7M,N.

claim: Prazosin decreased the locomotor activity of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the open field test.
source: Both prazosin and SCH23390 decreased the locomotor activity and traveling speed of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the open field test (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: SCH23390 decreased the locomotor activity of Th-Cre;Erbb4loxp/loxp mice in the open field test.
